newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Competition in packaging weighs on CHH.
newsitem.headline: Competition in packaging weighs on CHH.

text.p: Increased competition in the domestic packaging and packaging materials market was one of the reasons behind a slump in Carter Holt Harvey Ltd's (CHH) share price over recent days, analysts said on Thursday.

International Paper controlled CHH traded on Thursday at NZ$2.97, down six cents on Wednesday's close and down 18 cents since the start of the week. It is at its lowest since January 1996 and compares with a peak last June of $3.58.
Other factors likely to have depressed the stock were those afflicting others in the yield-sensitive forestry sector - high bond yields and low log and pulp prices.

But in CHH's case, the market's attention had turned to increased competition after the introduction of Visy to New Zealand last year, and to changes in supply arrangements with Amcor Ltd in the 200,000-tonne a year market.
John Cairns, head of research at Cavill White Securities, said it was not clear why Amcor would want to change the supply arrangement but it appeared to be linked to Visy's entry.
The upshot was that CHH would need to find a home for more product.
"I guess it's a reflection of the breakdown of a fairly cosy duopoly into a market that has become increasingly competitive," Cairns said.
CHH spokeswoman Jo Curin was unavailable for comment on the Amcor move.
Visy, part of Australia's the privately owned Pratt Industries Ltd, plans capacity to produce 40,000 tonnes of packaging a year but is understood to be well-short of that now.

"What we have seen is competition intensify in the packaging industry," said David Stanley, forestry analyst at Doyle Paterson Brown. The response to that from CHH was to rationalise is own packaging operations.
CHH had previously supplied packaging materials to the two major players -- its own Carter Holt Packaging and Amcor's Kiwi Packaging.
At the same time, the Australian packaging industry - dominated by Amcor and Visy - had become extremely competitive.

"Given that CHH has also said that they want to increase their share of packaging supplied into the Australian market, it's been clear for some time that there will be changes in the flows of supply from the various parties within the New Zealand and Australian packaging industries," Stanley said.
Amcor had been sending an increased portion of its production of linerboard and corrugating medium material from Australia to supply Kiwi.

How much the CHH-Kiwi contract arrangements had changed was not clear, but it meant CHH was now needed to export more. At the same time, New Zealand had seen a significant decline in packaging prices.

The changes had occurred more quickly than anticipated, causing a revision of analysts' estimates, Stanley said. Brokers were now shaving about NZ$5 million from their annual net profit after tax estimates for CHH.

"In the whole scheme of things I guess it's probably a few cents a share, but if it's the main reason for the recent decline in the CHH share price then that reaction is overdone in our opinion," he said.
Visy had secured contracts with Lion Nathan Ltd and Fisher and Paykel Ltd but had otherwise made slow progress in New Zealand.
